pulls.title: Expand and elaborate
pulls.author: chris-wood
pulls.body: This change integrates guiding principles, expands the architectural concepts, gives more deployment shapes, and provides moderation guidance. It expands the musings I put together and, with the help of Claude, provides a more thorough exploration of the deployment topologies. I made an attempt at reframing the core position of the draft too, moving away from rate limiting and towards the balance of attribution and private authentication.

pulls.title: Reorient around attribution and authorization
pulls.author: chris-wood
pulls.body: More work to be done still. I think we should add multiple request flows, one describing MOLE+WBA (for limiting basic public resource access) and then another for agents accessing a permissioned API (showing how they use WAG and maybe ID-JAG, depending on use case). Thoughts?

reviews.author: thibmeu
reviews.body: overall the two flows seem great. as a general comment, we should move away from the "human" topic. i don't think it helps. a principal and it's agent(s) seem much better

comments.body: note that DPOP does not fully address this. an intermediary can still alter the request body. client certificate (which i assume you would use with mTLS) simply stop at intermediaries. It feels that HTTP Message Signature with Content-Digest/Repr-Digest/whatever digest would help here.

i'm not sure that's true. MOLE may indeed be tied to a human subject (i don't like that term as we are discussing bits and electric impulses), but nothing prevents one principal to have multiple budgets depending on the number of agents for instance. the binding between MOLE-to-OAuth is still relevant. maybe something along the line

`MOLE adds no subject unlinkability on requests already identifying that subject`, which does not mean it's not useful
for this section, i liked the previous wording as to how the client experienced continuity while the site did not have linkability
on another note: we'll need to have a clear "MOLE(U)"
